summary: Extends OSPF so one physical link can be shared by several areas, letting the link count as an intra-area link in each. That gives an intra-area path in every area using the link. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Normally one road belongs to one neighborhood. This lets the same road count as part of several neighborhoods at once.

questions: can an ospf link be in multiple areas
what is an ospf multi-area adjacency
why are intra-area ospf paths preferred
subtitle: How two OSPF routers can share one physical link across several areas, so it counts as an inside path in each.

tldr.problem: A fast link between two Area Border Routers belongs to only one OSPF area, so traffic in another area keeps taking slower intra-area links because OSPF prefers intra-area paths over inter-area paths.
tldr.mechanism: The routers set up an extra adjacency per additional area over the same link. Each one is modeled as a point-to-point link in its area and advertised as a type 1 link in the Router LSA, with no type 3 link.
tldr.outcome: The link becomes an intra-area path in every area that uses it. The change is backward compatible with standard OSPF and also applies to OSPFv3.

today: RFC 5185 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Link Needs Several Areas
sections.content:
Sometimes an OSPF link should sit in more than one area. The RFC's example is a high-speed link between two Area Border Routers (ABRs), R1 and R2, that belongs to the backbone while both routers also connect to Area 1 through slower links via R3 and R4.

In the OSPF specification (RFC 2328), intra-area paths are preferred over inter-area paths. So R1 always sends traffic for R4 through Area 1 over the lower-speed links, and even uses the Area 1 path through R3 to reach Area 1 networks attached to R2. An OSPF virtual link cannot fix this without moving the R1-R2 link into Area 1, which is not desirable if it is really part of the backbone.
sections.eli5: Two towns have a fast highway between them, but the map says highway trips between neighborhoods are worse than back roads inside one neighborhood. So everyone takes the slow back roads.

sections.title: Alternatives Considered
sections.content:
The RFC lists other ways to get a link into several areas and why each falls short.

  • Secondary addresses: a separate OSPF interface per area on a numbered interface. This needs extra IP address configuration, does not work for unnumbered interfaces, and the extra addresses make the routing table larger.
  • One address, many areas: this would put the interface's subnet in several areas, which is contrary to the definition of an OSPF area as a collection of subnets.
  • Unnumbered links in many areas: the area ID can already be used to demultiplex received packets, but multi-access networks are not supported, and network management policies may not allow unnumbered links.
sections.eli5: Other fixes were like giving the road a second street name, or pretending one house is in two towns. Each one caused its own mess.

sections.title: The Multi-Area Adjacency Idea
sections.content:
ABRs simply establish multiple adjacencies that belong to different areas. Each multi-area adjacency is announced as a point-to-point link in its configured area, giving that area a topological path. Unlike numbered point-to-point links, no type 3 link is advertised for it.

The first, or primary, adjacency on the link works and is advertised as RFC 2328 describes. Multi-area adjacencies are configured between two routers that share an interface. On point-to-point interfaces the neighbor address need not be configured. On other network types it must be configured or discovered by a mechanism external to OSPF.
sections.eli5: Instead of moving the road, the two towns agree to count it as theirs in each map, one extra handshake per map.

sections.title: Sending, Receiving and Advertising
sections.content:
On point-to-point interfaces, control packets go to the AllSPFRouters address. On all other network types they are unicast to the remote neighbor's IP address.

The RFC changes the packet checks of Section 8.2 of RFC 2328. The Area ID in the header must match the receiving interface's area, or indicate a non-backbone area that matches a configured multi-area adjacency, or indicate the backbone (virtual link or multi-area adjacency). A packet that matches a configured multi-area adjacency is associated with it from then on. A match for both a virtual link and a multi-area adjacency is a configuration error.

Each configured adjacency gets its own interface data structure, always of type point-to-point, and the interface and neighbor state machines are those of a point-to-point link. Once the adjacency reaches the FULL state it is added to the Router LSA as a link type 1, with Link ID set to the remote router's Router ID and Link Data set to the neighbor's IP address, or its IfIndex if the interface is unnumbered.
sections.eli5: Each handshake carries the name of its neighborhood. The router reads the name, files the message under the right map, and only then adds the road to that map.

sections.title: Compatibility and OSPFv3
sections.content:
Everything here is backward compatible with standard OSPF implementations. Because the adjacency looks like a point-to-point link, only the router at the other end has to model it that way, although symmetric configuration makes the topology easier to represent and troubleshoot.

The mechanism also applies to OSPFv3. The link is advertised as a point-to-point link in the router-LSA, but the Link Data change above is not needed, since OSPFv3 router-LSA links do not depend on addressing. No prefixes for the adjacency go into the intra-area-prefix-LSA, and a link-LSA SHOULD NOT be advertised for it. The neighbor's IPv6 link-local address can be learned another way, for example from the IPv6 header of received Hello packets.
sections.eli5: A neighbor that has never heard of this trick still understands a plain road sign, so nothing breaks.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that it raises no security issues beyond those already covered in OSPF (RFC 2328) and OSPFv3 (RFC 2740).
sections.eli5: Nothing new to worry about beyond the usual OSPF rules.
